## Introduction

In recent years, society has stood divided on remote work. Some claim that remote work causes work productivity to slip due to distractions, home activities, etc, while others, have claimed that they feel they are able to work more productively than in the office because they can deal with their home life and work life at the same time. This introduces a question, who is right?

In this paper, I attempt to see if remote work reduces productivity compared to in-person work. I will use an online data set from Kaggle to get my results. I hypothesize that remote work will reduce self-perceived productivity.

## Methods

In order to conduct this experiment, I will use results from the Kaggle online data set to create comparisons between remote work respondents and office work respondents. I will specifically focus on the variable: Do you think that working from home increases your work productivity? Additionally, the data set has occupations, years in the workforce, and age group which can also be used to find results. I will use R Studio to do my analyses. 

In my analysis, I intend to compare whether job occupation impacts remote work productivity, whether age impacts remote work productivity, and whether years in the workforce impact work productivity. By comparing these groups, we can find out if productivity is either reduced or increased based on several factors. With the results of these analyses, I will be able to answer my hypothesis, and make suggestions for future research.

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(tidyverse)
set.seed(123)   # makes simulated p-values reproducible

df <- read.csv("The Impacts of Working Remotely and in an Office Survey 2.csv") %>%
  rename(productivity = Do.you.think.that.working.from.home.increases.your.work.productivity.,
         arrangement  = Current.Work.Arrangement,
         experience   = Years.of.Experience,
         age          = Age.Group,
         industry     = Industry,
         gender       = Gender)

# Order the age/experience groups correctly (sorted by the first number in each label)
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    prod_bin   = as.integer(productivity == "Yes"),
    age        = factor(age, levels = unique(age)[order(parse_number(unique(age)))]),
    experience = factor(experience, levels = unique(experience)[order(parse_number(unique(experience)))]),
    age_num    = as.numeric(age),
    exp_num    = as.numeric(experience)
  )

# Cramér's V (effect size) without needing extra packages
cramers_v <- function(tab) {
  chi <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab, correct = FALSE))$statistic
  unname(sqrt(chi / (sum(tab) * (min(dim(tab)) - 1))))
}
```
```{r}
#| label: chi-square

# Main test in detail: work arrangement vs. productivity
tab <- table(df$arrangement, df$productivity)
tab                                # counts
round(prop.table(tab, 1), 3)       # row percentages
main_test <- chisq.test(tab)
main_test                          # chi-square, df, p-value
round(main_test$expected, 1)       # check assumption: expected counts >= 5
round(main_test$stdres, 2)         # standardized residuals (beyond ±2 = notable)
cramers_v(tab)                     # effect size

# Same test for every predictor, in one table
run_chisq <- function(data, var) {
  tab  <- table(data[[var]], data$productivity)
  test <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab))
  simulated <- min(test$expected) < 5          # fall back to simulation if cells are small
  if (simulated) test <- chisq.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 10000)
  tibble(Predictor = var,
         N         = sum(tab),
         ChiSq     = round(unname(test$statistic), 2),
         df        = if (simulated) NA_real_ else unname(test$parameter),
         p         = test$p.value,
         CramersV  = round(cramers_v(tab), 3),
         Simulated = simulated)
}

chisq_results <- map_dfr(c("arrangement", "industry", "experience", "age"),
                         ~ run_chisq(df, .x)) %>%
  mutate(p_holm = p.adjust(p, method = "holm"))   # correct for multiple tests
chisq_results

# Which arrangements differ from each other?
pairwise.prop.test(table(df$arrangement, df$productivity)[, "Yes"],
                   rowSums(table(df$arrangement, df$productivity)),
                   p.adjust.method = "holm")

# Residuals for industry (shows which industries drive the result)
round(chisq.test(table(df$industry, df$productivity))$stdres, 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: trend-tests

# Does the odds of "Yes" rise or fall steadily across ordered groups?
age_trend <- glm(prod_bin ~ age_num, data = df, family = binomial)
exp_trend <- glm(prod_bin ~ exp_num, data = df, family = binomial)

summary(age_trend)$coefficients   # significant age_num = linear trend with age
summary(exp_trend)$coefficients   # significant exp_num = linear trend with experience
```

```{r}
#| label: logistic-regression

# All predictors together; reference group for arrangement = Fully In-Office
df$arrangement <- relevel(factor(df$arrangement), ref = "Fully In-Office")

m <- glm(prod_bin ~ arrangement + experience + industry + age + gender,
         data = df, family = binomial)
summary(m)

# Odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals
or_table <- exp(cbind(OR = coef(m), suppressMessages(confint(m))))
round(or_table, 2)

# Does the full model beat an empty model?
anova(m, test = "Chisq")
```

```{r}
#| label: remote-only

remote_only <- df %>% filter(arrangement == "Fully Remote")

map_dfr(c("age", "experience"), ~ run_chisq(remote_only, .x))
```
